title: Elekta Began as a Student's Tax Idea in His Father's Flat
dek: In 1972 a business student incorporated his father's inventions to save tax; for a decade the company that would sell the Gamma Knife barely sold anything.

story.event: Incorporating Elekta around Lars Leksell's inventions, and its slow first decade
story.summary: On 10 October 1972 Larry Leksell, a first-year student at the Stockholm School of Economics, incorporated Elekta around the patents of his father, the neurosurgeon Lars Leksell, mainly to reduce tax and free money for research; at the time there was one Gamma Knife in the world and the company lived on royalties from the stereotactic frame. Run unpaid by the family from Lars Leksell's flat, it stayed tiny for a decade, was saved from near-bankruptcy in 1979 by Larry's personal bank loan, and signed its first Gamma Knife sale in its own name, with a Pittsburgh hospital, late in 1986.
paragraphs: In the early 1970s the world had one Gamma Knife. Lars Leksell, professor of neurosurgery at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, had developed it with the radiobiologist Börje Larsson to treat targets deep in the brain with converging beams of cobalt-60 radiation instead of an open operation; the prototype treated its first patient in 1967. Leksell had little interest in selling: colleagues wanting his stereotactic frame were sent to the workshop that made it, and he reckoned three to five Gamma Knives would meet the world's needs.

The idea of a company came from his son Laurent, known as Larry, then in his first year at the Stockholm School of Economics, at a time when, he later recalled, the marginal tax on personal income was ninety per cent. Leksell already traded as a one-man firm called Elekta, from the Greek for chosen; Larry pointed out that a limited company would cut the tax bill, free income for research and make grants easier to win. His father agreed, provided he could keep researching. The company was registered on 10 October 1972. "Basically," Larry said decades later, "the formation of Elekta was based on tax planning."

It was a family affair: Larry as unpaid chief executive, his elder brother Dan, a medical student, as unpaid medical adviser, and Dan's wife working part-time from a room in their father's flat on Strandvägen. Dan later said the company at first "had nothing to do with Gamma Knife." Its income was royalties on the frame.

The next decade was slow. A second Gamma Knife went into the Karolinska Hospital in 1974, largely paid for by a research foundation rather than sold, and turnover after two years was 200,000 kronor. Each machine would cost a hospital three to four million dollars, and the workshop that built the first two fell into crisis. In 1979, with the company near bankruptcy, Larry took a personal bank loan of 300,000 kronor and, with his siblings' agreement, took over the whole company. By 1982 it still had one salaried employee.
Lars Leksell died in January 1986. Larry then left his own consultancy to run Elekta full time, and late that year it signed its first Gamma Knife sale in its own name, with a hospital in Pittsburgh.

quote.text: If the search for riches is sure to be successful, though I should become a groom with whip in hand to get them, I will do so. As the search may not be successful, I will follow after that which I love.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Confucius would chase riches only if success were sure; since it is not, he follows what he loves. Leksell kept to the research he loved and left the uncertain search for income to his son, and for a decade that search looked every bit as unpromising as Confucius warned.

reflection: It is tempting to think a company needs a grand origin. Elekta's was a registration form filed by a student so that his father could go on with the work he loved, and for ten years little happened. What kept it alive was a handful of people doing unglamorous things: keeping the books, answering letters about a frame, taking a loan when one was needed.

In that family the love of the work and the search for income lived in different people, and each made room for the other. You may be carrying both at once. On the days the income side looks uncertain, it can help to name plainly which part of the work you would keep doing anyway.
invitation: Write one sentence naming the part of your work you would keep doing even if it never paid. Put it somewhere you will see it on a slower week.

cross_checks.claim: Elekta was incorporated in 1972 by Larry Leksell, then a student at the Stockholm School of Economics, around his father's inventions
The company was formed mainly to reduce tax and release income for research
At the start Elekta lived on royalties from the stereotactic instrument, not on Gamma Knife sales
Lars Leksell died in 1986, after which Larry went full time

research_notes: The slate described this as Lars Leksell 'founding a company to make the Gamma Knife'. The sources say otherwise, and the story follows them: Elekta's own history says Lars Leksell did not found or run the company, which his son Larry created for him 'primarily for practical fiscal reasons'; Dan Leksell says it 'had nothing to do with Gamma Knife' at first; Larry himself calls it tax planning. The Centre for Business History's announcement and Wikipedia instead say Lars founded it with Larry to commercialise or 'exploit' the Gamma Knife; the story keeps both men as founders but describes the company's actual early business. Larry's stage of study: Elekta says he was 20 and finishing his first year; Larry says 'my first semester'; the story says 'in his first year'. Early revenue: Elekta gives turnover of 200,000 SEK after two years; Cancerworld paraphrases Larry as 'a few hundred thousand dollars' from frames and royalties without a date; the story uses Elekta's dated figure. Pittsburgh: Cancerworld has Larry saying the first US Gamma Knife was installed in 1986 and that his father died three months after its inauguration, and Wikipedia also says 1986; Elekta's history, written from its archive, says the contract was signed in late 1986, after Lars Leksell's death in January 1986, and that the first Pittsburgh operation was in August 1987. Lars Leksell's death in 1986 is consistent across Elekta, Cérebro & Mente and Wikipedia, so the Cancerworld sequence is treated as a slip of memory (it may conflate the Sheffield installation) and the story says only that the contract was signed late in 1986. Elekta's history was commissioned by Elekta but researched and written by the Centre for Business History; it is cited as a company archive. Funding is set to 'bootstrapped' (the slate said 'mixed'): the company ran on royalties, unpaid family labour and Larry's personal bank loan; the first two Gamma Knife units were funded largely by the Axel Johnson Foundation, outside the company, and the Pittsburgh deal later needed a guarantee from the state-owned Investeringsbanken. Elekta's history says that in 1982 Stockholm was still the only location for a Gamma Knife in the world, but its next chapter says the 1967 prototype had been shipped to UCLA for experimental use in 1981, so the story drops the claim. Confucius's saying is about his own choices; it is applied to the division of roles between father and son by analogy.
